title: How Buildering Works
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck open with a promo for Chuck's new solo podcast Movie Crush, then discuss buildering, the sport of climbing buildings, blending "building" and "bouldering." They trace its history from Cambridge University roof climbers (Geoffrey Winthrop Young's guidebook to Trinity College, and Noel Symington's "The Night Climbers of Cambridge," which coined "night climbing") to American human flies such as Harry H. Gardner in the 1910s, who climbed Detroit, Birmingham, and Vancouver buildings before vanishing and possibly being murdered in Paris. They cover Henry Roland's Iowa courthouse climbs, H.F. Young's fatal fall, city crackdowns, the distinction between urban climbing and buildering, George Willig's 1977 World Trade Center climb, Dan Goodwin's Spider-Man-costumed climbs of Chicago and Toronto buildings, Alain Robert's climbs and arrests, stunt work in Casino Royale and Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol, the dangers and liability issues, and a listener mail about dozing off while reading.

segments.title: Movie Crush promo and opening banter
segments.summary: Chuck promotes his new solo podcast Movie Crush and asks for guests. The hosts then banter about movies, including Man on Wire and special effects.

segments.title: Episode intro and definition of buildering
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and explain that buildering combines building and bouldering to mean climbing the outside of buildings, usually illegally.

segments.title: Early history: Cambridge roof climbers
segments.summary: Geoffrey Winthrop Young wrote a guide to climbing Trinity College buildings in Cambridge, England. Noel Symington later wrote The Night Climbers of Cambridge and is credited with coining night climbing.

segments.title: Harry Gardner and early American human flies
segments.summary: Skyscrapers in the early twentieth century brought American building climbers. Harry H. Gardner climbed the Detroit News building in 1916 at midday, then buildings in Birmingham and Vancouver. He disappeared and was possibly murdered in Paris.

segments.title: Henry Roland, H.F. Young, and city crackdowns
segments.summary: Henry Roland climbed the Davis County Courthouse in Iowa after an injury and returned to climb it again. H.F. Young died falling from the Hotel Martinique. Cities then moved to stop the climbs.

segments.title: Urban climbing vs. buildering and George Willig's World Trade Center climb
segments.summary: The hosts distinguish urban climbing, which can use cranes or bridges, from buildering, which uses only the facade. George Willig climbed the World Trade Center in 1977 with homemade devices, was arrested, and became famous.

segments.title: Dan Goodwin, Spider-Man costume climbs, and Alain Robert
segments.summary: Dan Goodwin climbed Chicago's Sears Tower and John Hancock Tower in a Spider-Man costume, and the CN Tower in Toronto twice in one day. Alain Robert became well known in the mid-1990s and has been arrested many times. Robert has used banners for sponsorship and climate messages.

segments.title: Film stunts, legality, liability, and the Man on Wire comparison
segments.summary: The hosts discuss buildering stunts in Casino Royale and Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol, the arrests and restraining orders, property liability, and the danger of falls. They also cover Dan Goodwin's claims about the Chicago fire department and his 1980s motivation after a hotel fire.

segments.title: Inspirations, recent climbs, and deaths
segments.summary: The hosts list climbers' inspirations, including Zorro and Robin Hood, and mention the 2008 New York Times building climb. Ryan John Hartley died in Houston in 2003 in a fall that witnesses said was intentional.

segments.title: Listener mail: dozing off while reading
segments.summary: Listener Harrison Gibbs asks why he falls asleep while reading. The hosts suggest a paper book instead of a screen before bed. They close with social media and website info.
